newsitem.title: UK: Europe crude outlook - Stagnant unless arb opens.
newsitem.headline: Europe crude outlook - Stagnant unless arb opens.

text.p: European crudes will struggle to move higher this week and could stagnate at depressed levels unless export opportunities to the U.S. improve, traders said.

While an overhang of end September cargoes was virtually cleared out last week and European refiners margins are holding up well, the lack of a workable arbitrage to the U.S. is keeping a lid on wet market differentials.
"The States would dearly like some of this oil but it's too expensive for them at the moment," said a trader.
"They're going to have to buy but it won't happen until somebody is really squeezed and they have to start buying up the WTI because it's all they can get hold of," he added.

The Brent-WTI spread widened last week to around $1.15 a barrel but traders said it would need to improve by a further 20 cents or so before barrels start to flow regularly into the U.S., relieving pressure on sloppy northwest European markets.
Dated Brent traded at a weak Oct Brent less 48 cents a barrel on Friday and while the benchmark grade was unlikely to suffer further falls, it's room to the upside was also limited, traders said.
"There are still two or three (Brents) left at the end of the month and then you have the early October barrels," said a trader.

All five of Friday's Brent cargoes were kept on Friday by British Petroleum. Traders said BP would be seeking to profit from operational tolerance in the system and the move did not reflect a rise in end-user demand for the crude.
Other North Sea crudes, particularly the lighter grades, were also unlikely to recover much from recent low levels.
Late Sept Ekofisk traded at a two-cent discount to Dated on Friday after a Forties deal Thursday at Dated plus seven cents.
"If I add up the demand I can see against what's left in the programme it doesn't look too great," said an oil major trader.
"There has been a bit of a clear out of (Oct) 1-10 barrels but we could just see a standoff this week as sellers raise their numbers and buyers continue to hang back," said another.
Sellers said one ray of hope was a sustained improvement in margins -- the Brent-gas oil crack spread remains around $5.90 a barrel - but even that was only benefitting certain crudes.
"Maybe people will start buying a little more but all that has happened so far is that distillate-rich crudes like West African have been sucked in," said a trader.
A recent surge in gas oil prices on the back of low stocks and the approach of winter has improved Med refiners margins.
Russian Urals was sold out for September and refiners keenly awaited the October loading programme, expected later this week, traders said.
"Refiners are scrambling around for what they can find. There's no Urals and they're having to buy sweet," said one.

Nigerian crudes were expected to benefit further from demand for blending with sour to cut the sulphur content of gas oil ahead of the October 1 deadline for Europe's switch to 0.05 percent sulphur diesel. -- London Newsroom +44 171 542 7930
